question: A day after full moon, the Moon still looks fully lit. How much of its light has already gone?
answer: About a quarter. At full moon the Sun sits right behind the observer, so every grain of lunar dust hides its own shadow and light scatters straight back. A little off that line, shadows reappear all over the face. From quarter to full the lit area only doubles, while the brightness rises about tenfold.
move: When an effect far outruns its obvious cause, look for a second mechanism.
ask: When an effect is much bigger than its obvious cause, what second cause am I missing?
reference: Hapke, Nelson & Smythe, The Opposition Effect of the Moon: The Contribution of Coherent Backscatter, Science, 1993; Allen's Astrophysical Quantities, 4th edition, ed. Cox, Springer, 2000 (lunar phase curve)

notes.text: Full moon: the Sun is behind you, and every grain hides its own shadow.
One day off full: 99% of the face lit, a quarter of the light gone.
Halfway to the quarter: 85% lit, a third of the light.
Quarter moon: half the face lit, a tenth of the light.
